A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpatialScore/SpatialAgent research project, and their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison. The redesigned benchmark and protocols limit direct score comparisons, rather than document comparability.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of MLLMs and SpatialAgent on VGBench, SpatialScore, and SpatialScore-Hard, with additional source-dataset results in Appendix F.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, human and text-only controls, supervised fine-tuning results, SpatialAgent comparisons, and additional subset and failure analyses.

M1.justification: V2 adds supervised fine-tuning on SpatialCorpus using cross-entropy, absent from v1. SpatialAgent retains Plan-Execute and ReAct but substantially changes its toolbox: Rex-Omni replaces OWLv2 localization and supports counting, while DetAny3D and MapAnything add 3D detection and metric-distance capabilities (Sections 3.2–3.4).

E1.justification: Coverage expands from 11 integrated datasets to 23, adding tasks such as maze navigation, paper folding, mental rotation, velocity estimation, and size compatibility. V2 also introduces real-world and simulated training coverage through SpatialCorpus. Geometry tasks persist within the repurposed data; that component adds Omni3D and PointOdyssey and stops sourcing ScanNet.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparators including Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, SpaceThinker, and SpaceR, while Cambrian-8B and SpatialBot-Phi2 disappear from the quantitative comparisons. Proprietary comparisons shift from GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Haiku, and Gemini-2.0-Flash to newer systems. Human, random, and text-only baselines are also added.

E3.justification: V1's 28,093 samples and 1,400-sample Hard subset give way to 5,025 samples selected using text-only filtering and manual verification. SpatialScore numerical scoring changes from factor-two tolerance to MRA with parser/LLM score averaging; MRA already appeared in v1's separate VSI-Bench evaluation. Video sampling changes from eight frames by default to 32 for open models and 16/8 for proprietary models. The agent token limit increases from 2,048 to 4,096.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Figure 4 cases, v2 adds annotation-error examples (Figure 5), analyses of fine-tuning versus agent generalization across OpenSource and Repurpose subsets (Appendix C.1), quantitative reasoning-failure analysis (Appendix B.3), and new qualitative cases (Figures 9–10). These provide substantial new evidence about data quality, distribution dependence, and agent reliability.

E5.justification: Both versions specify a fixed random seed and deterministic decoding. Neither reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's human-participant count and agent failure percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and source-dataset result tables are replaced by results for the redesigned benchmark and new training/agent comparisons. For example, v2 Table 3 reports Qwen3-VL-8B scores of 45.48 zero-shot, 54.71 after fine-tuning, and 53.81 with ReAct; Table 2 adds human performance of 86.60. These are newly reported results under revised conditions, not direct gains over v1's scores.

T1.justification: The Plan-Execute and ReAct mathematical formulations remain equivalent apart from notation and explicit backbone bookkeeping. Neither version develops theorems or proofs. V2's standard fine-tuning description and MRA scoring instructions add method and evaluation documentation rather than substantive mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds VGBench as the first dedicated visual-geometry benchmark, the 28K SpatialScore collection and Hard subset, and SpatialAgent. V2 redefines the central contributions around a curated 30-task benchmark, the 331K SpatialCorpus training resource, and complementary fine-tuning and expanded agent approaches. VGBench and SpatialScore-Hard cease to be separately claimed contributions.

C2.justification: V2 attributes larger fine-tuning gains on Repurpose to training-distribution alignment, discusses potential forgetting and uneven task improvements, and adds limitations concerning SpatialCorpus diversity. It also interprets measured failure rates as evidence of ReAct's greater stability. The RGB-input and rudimentary-toolbox limitations already existed in v1; their relocation to Section 7 is not a new limitation.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new fine-tuning recipe: one epoch, batch size 512, learning rate 1e-5, 3% warm-up, and a frozen visual encoder. It expands construction templates, distractor rules, scoring prompts, and tool specifications, and reports eight rather than four A100 GPUs. Explicit code and dataset links are added, although the PDFs do not establish actual resource availability.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands engagement with recent spatial benchmarks, training approaches, and perception tools, including SpatialEval, OmniSpatial, SPAR-Bench, MMSI-Bench, Rex-Omni, and MapAnything. The new benchmark-comparison Table 1 and revised related work position the contribution as a comprehensive evaluation and improvement framework, replacing the earlier emphasis on VGBench's visual-geometry novelty.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and substantial portions of the main text are rewritten. Baseline evaluation moves into the benchmark section, methodology is reorganized around two improvement approaches, limitations move into the main text, and six appendix sections are reorganized into three. This exceeds renaming or routine editing.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, construction pipeline, toolbox diagram, and dataset-flow visualization. Result tables adopt new task columns, grouping, rankings, and highlighting; benchmark-comparison, annotation-error, and additional qualitative displays are added. Figure 4 is substantially retained and relocated, while the document typography, prompt boxes, and page layout are extensively reformatted.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation validity through annotation-error auditing, visual-dependence filtering, full-set manual verification, and explicit human/text-only controls, addressing weaknesses left open in v1. Detailed fine-tuning experiments, source-dependent generalization analysis, and quantified agent failures also deepen the evidence beyond headline accuracy. These gains outweigh the loss of source-by-source result tables. Some reporting inconsistencies remain: Appendix C.1 uses 48.72 as the starting point for an agent improvement, although Table 6 identifies that as the fine-tuned score and gives 42.97 for zero-shot.
